doc.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009

title: Grimes's years away from music and poetry
summary: Grimes listened to Tex-Mex rather than jazz, wrote poetry, and returned to a new recording world.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Yeah. Neat. Henry, the years you spent out of the music business, were you still listening to music? Did you have an opportunity to listen to what was going on?
I wasn’t, no. I was listening to Texas Mexican music.
Or I’d listen to a lot of — what’s the name of that other kind of Mexican music where there are seven different kinds of music that they play.
Yeah, Mariachi. And a lot of Chinese and all things like that, all kinds of things like that. Or different kinds of — but my favorite was the Texas Mex.
Tex Mex music. I’ll be darned.
But you know I used to listen to that. But I didn’t have — all I had was a TV and sometimes I’d catch some things on TV maybe slightly, but very, very slightly, because of what I had on my mind.
Okay. Were you surprised at the change in technology when you eventually went back into the studio to record and what had happened with how things are done?

No, I’m not that aware of it. Just like a lot of technology that has occurred between then and now, and also, well for many years it’s always been a thing of technology and sounds and electronics and hooked up with music.
The years when you weren’t playing, is that when your poetry really became a vital part of what you were doing?

Yeah, when I had nothing to do, like I quit that, and I write poetry. And sometimes I might be thinking about like how do I favor a beat or something like that, but that was just an idea to make music but also all kinds of metric ideas you know. Poetry or music. But I wasn’t listening to music at that time, so that was a long time ago, that was about 30 years.
Well you made a big impression when you came back.
Yeah. I know what you mean.
